props.title: Now You See Him, Now You Don't

sections.content: Disney's 1970s live-action comedies hit their stride with Now You See Him, Now You Don't (1972), starring Kurt Russell in his third collaboration with director Robert Butler. This invisible man comedy follows the success of The Computer Wore Tennis Shoes (1969), cementing Russell's transition from child actor to leading man. The film cleverly adapts H.G. Wells' invisible man concept for family audiences, trading horror for slapstick while maintaining the core premise of scientific discovery gone awry.

sections.content: The invisible effects in Now You See Him, Now You Don't showcase Disney's practical effects mastery during a transitional period in special effects history. While primitive by today's standards, the wire work and black velvet techniques created convincing invisibility years before digital effects. This approach influenced later invisible character films like Hollow Man (2000) and The Invisible (2007), though those films took darker approaches to the concept.

The campus setting and scientific discovery plot align with Disney's 1970s focus on youth-oriented stories mixing comedy with light sci-fi elements. This formula proved successful enough to spawn a third Kurt Russell vehicle, The Strongest Man in the World (1975), completing an unofficial trilogy of Medfield College adventures that helped define Disney's live-action identity in the decade. sections.content: Now You See Him, Now You Don't established a template for Disney science comedies that influenced films for decades. From Honey, I Shrunk the Kids (1989) to Flubber (1997), Disney consistently returned to the formula of likeable protagonists making accidental scientific breakthroughs with comedic consequences. The Medfield College setting itself became a recurring location in Disney films, representing an idealized academic environment where amazing discoveries could happen.
